name: Propagating tree
description: Iahub likes trees very much. Recently he discovered an interesting tree named propagating tree. The tree consists of n nodes numbered from 1 to n , each node i having an initial value a i . The root of the tree is node 1 . This tree has a special property: when a value val is added to a value of node i , the value - val is added to values of all the children of node i . Note that when you add value - val to a child of node i , you also add -(- val ) to all children of the child of node i and so on. Look an example explanation to understand better how it works. This tree supports two types of queries: " 1 x val " — val is added to the value of node x ; " 2 x " — print the current value of node x . In order to help Iahub understand the tree better, you must answer m queries of the preceding type.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers n and m (1 ≤ n , m ≤ 200000) . The second line contains n integers a 1 , a 2 , ..., a n (1 ≤ a i ≤ 1000) . Each of the next n –1 lines contains two integers v i and u i (1 ≤ v i , u i ≤ n ) , meaning that there is an edge between nodes v i and u i . Each of the next m lines contains a query in the format described above. It is guaranteed that the following constraints hold for all queries: 1 ≤ x ≤ n , 1 ≤ val ≤ 1000 .
output_specification: For each query of type two (print the value of node x ) you must print the answer to the query on a separate line. The queries must be answered in the order given in the input.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 383C — Propagating tree [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
